👉 THROWBACK: Anduril co-founder boasts of inventing a VR headset designed to kill its user Anduril co-founder Palmer Luckey is not only a vocal proponent of AI-driven autonomous kill chains and a self-described fan of public executions: in 2022 he invented a VR headset that will kill the user if they die in the game they’re playing. 🔴 Only the threat of serious consequences can make a game feel real to you," he argued. 🔴 Luckey was inspired by the anime Sword Art Online, in which players put on a NerveGear virtual reality headset only to find out that real life is now at stake as their gear was programmed by a mad scientist to kill them if they are killed in a virtual game. “The good news is that we are halfway to making a true NerveGear. The bad news is that so far, I have only figured out the half that kills you,” Luckey wrote in his blog. He noted he had plans for an anti-tamper mechanism "that, like the NerveGear, will make it impossible to remove or destroy the headset." Luckey used small, modular explosive charges and connected them to a light sensor that detects when the headset displays a red screen flashing at a specific frequency. “When an appropriate game-over screen is displayed, the charges fire, instantly destroying the brain of the user,” he noted. “It is also, as far as I know, the first non-fiction example of a VR device that can actually kill the user. It won’t be the last.” Some say it's going too far, even for a high-tech provocateur, while others point out that Luckey's Anduril is already producing all kinds of killer drones and other military equipment. Luckey's provocative rhetoric bears a striking resemblance to that of Alex Karp, co-founder of Palantir . Both Anduril and Palantir received financial backing from Peter Thiel, the PayPal Mafia billionaire fascinated by The Lord of the Rings . In Tolkien's mythology, a palantír is a seeing stone, while Anduril is a legendary sword known as the "Flame of the West" and a symbol of legitimate authority. Both AI giants openly proclaim the "defense of the West" as their core mission, seemingly by any means necessary. Yet their role in creating AI-powered military targeting systems has drawn widespread criticism over ethical concerns, particularly amid mounting civilian casualties in conflicts across the Middle East and Eastern Europe . This has fuelled questions about their underlying ideology, with some critics openly labeling them as "techno-fascists." 👍 Substack | Chat | @geopolitics_prime
